section_map.summary: The Summary defines the river, demand, campsite collision rule, three scheduling goals, priority mechanism, paced movement, campsite-night efficiency benchmark, discrete magic-number claim, sensitivity findings, strengths, weaknesses, and future work before the detailed paper begins.

The Memo tells managers that advance reservations enable the scheduler, claims high trip volume and minimal interaction, equates the stated capacity with campsite count, and gives a two-condition magic-number rule as the operating action.
The Introduction restates the 225-mile, two-craft, six-to-eighteen-night problem and joins throughput, nightly campsite feasibility, and limited contact in one compact objective.

The assumptions fix the season, equally spaced campsites, a minimum site count, downstream-only movement, advance requests, daily travel hours, trip-length distributions, and motor-oar mixture, with a short rationale and computational consequence for each.

The analysis separates completed trips, crossovers, and rescheduling, contrasts pre-scheduled and first-come demand, and proposes least-days-left plus low-mobility priority as the organizing hypothesis.
The model maps each trip to a Boat state, the river to an ordered campsite set, daily reach to a floor bound, and the season to a two-dimensional schedule consumed by Java Boat and River classes.

The scheduler builds each day from a priority queue, computes a preferred site, handles completion, direct placement, upstream fallback, and recursive role swapping, then launches new boats and removes season-end nonfinishers.

The improvement stage adds a movement constant, specifies first-come launch placement, deletes and requeues late boats, and proposes best-of-many random schedules when managers predefine the trip inventory.

The results connect a positive movement constant to more completions and fewer reschedules, interpret floor-function jumps as magic or black-magic settings, and compare simulated trips with a campsite-night efficiency reference.

The sensitivity section varies travel time, motor fraction, duration distribution, season length, river length, and campsite count, reporting smooth trends interrupted by discrete reachability thresholds.
The paper credits high synthetic utilization and priority-induced crossover reduction, then acknowledges random launch order and occasional rescheduling and proposes preset trips plus rollback.

The conclusion converts the study into three operational rules: prioritize low remaining time, prefer the less mobile craft on ties, and tune travel time, campsite count, and river length to favorable discrete thresholds.
Five references provide river-camping context, Java data structures and APIs, daylight information, and rafting-duration context, but do not freeze model inputs or simulation outputs.

The appendix supplies complete Boat.java and River.java listings for state, priority, movement, launch placement, rescheduling, daily scheduling, schedule diagnostics, crossover counting, uniform and clipped-Gaussian request generation, and the interactive entry point.

assumptions.summary: The boating season runs April 1 through September 30, giving 183 days and 182 nights.
The 225-mile river has Y equally spaced campsites at distance 225/(Y+1).
At least eighteen campsites are available and one boat occupies a campsite per night.
Boats never move upstream and all requests are known sufficiently far in advance.
Daily travel time is a tunable six-to-twelve-hour parameter and craft demand is initially uniform and random.
Motor and oar request proportions may vary and later duration tests use craft-specific clipped Gaussian draws.
A boat is synonymous with one trip and is represented only by craft type, duration, remaining days, and current site.
Pre-scheduled trip inventories may be approximated by selecting the best of many random request sequences.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Problem constants supply 225 miles, 4 mph oar craft, 8 mph motor craft, six-to-eighteen-night requests, and one boat per campsite-night.
The movement-margin experiment reports 557.91 to 617.796 average trips and .793 to .166 average reschedules when adding one site of margin.
Figure 3 records rescheduled trips against campsite count and displays periodic threshold structure.
The preferred setting uses daily distance limits 80 and 40 miles, m_C=4, equal craft shares, uniform durations, and 44 sites.
The reported best result is 659.371 trips from ten data points of one thousand iterations, converted to about 98.8 percent.
Figure 4 plots trips per year against motor share with y=-26.173x^2+66.222x+617.96 and R^2=0.9968.
The Gaussian scenario uses printed means 12 and 13 nights in prose, while appendix code uses day parameters 13 and 14 with standard deviations 3 and 2 and clips to 7 through 19 days.
Five references provide contextual and software sources but no frozen empirical or computational dataset.

models.summary: Convert campsite count into the assumed uniform inter-site distance.
Bound daily site movement by craft speed, travel hours, and discretized river geometry.
Choose the minimum average campsite progress needed to exit on schedule.
Move faster than the bare average pace to free upstream sites and reduce lateness.
Detect an adjacent campsite-count setting where motor-boat daily reach increases by one site.
Require the motor reach to remain exactly twice the oar reach at the selected setting.
Compare approximate occupied campsite-nights with the seasonal campsite-night capacity.
Give a continuous average-length reference for the number of trips supported by available campsite-nights.
Represent one trip by craft type, identifier, total days, remaining days, and current campsite.
Store one Boat reference per day and campsite with a waiting queue, completed list, and trip and lateness counters.
Order boats by the fewest days remaining and use the implementation's craft-type comparator as the tie break.
For each day, collect yesterday's boats, move them in priority order, add new boats, and remove season-end nonfinishers.
Compute paced movement plus the movement margin, cap it by maximum daily reach, and add it to the current site.
When nextSite passes Final Exit, decrement remaining days, count an on-time completion, or delete and requeue a late trip.
Place the highest-priority boat directly when its preferred site is empty and update its day and site state.
Search from the preferred site back to the prior site and take the first empty campsite without moving upstream relative to yesterday.
Displace lower-priority boats or the boat at the previous site until the chain reaches an empty campsite.
Poll the request queue, reject trips that cannot finish before season end, and place each new boat at its preferred or nearest upstream open site.
Remove every historical schedule reference to a late boat, reset its state, and push it to the front of the queue.
Generate many random request sequences with fixed parameters and retain the schedule with the most completed trips.
Vary m_C and campsite count while comparing completed and rescheduled trips to choose a useful movement margin.
Sweep campsite count, travel time, and river length and locate floor-function reach changes associated with trip-count jumps.
Convert completed trips and average trip nights into an approximate campsite-night utilization percentage.
Vary travel time, motor fraction, duration distribution, season length, river length, and campsite count and compare trip totals.
Scan completed boats to print early, late, and excessive-movement counts.
Compare relative boat ordering on adjacent days and increment or cancel candidate overtaking events.
Generate two thousand motor or oar requests with integer trip lengths, run the scheduler, and print schedule and diagnostics.
Generate two thousand craft-specific Gaussian values clipped to seven through nineteen days, run the scheduler, and print diagnostics.
Read a distribution name and campsite count, dispatch one harness, or print an unknown-distribution message.

results_trace.summary: Adding m_C=1 raises average completed trips by about 10.7 percent and lowers average reschedules in the stated experiment.
Larger movement margins eventually raise rescheduling and are recommended at roughly eight to fifteen percent of maximum travel distance.
Magic campsite counts appear as periodic low-reschedule settings when daily reach floor values increase in aligned motor-oar steps.
At 8.8 travel hours the model retains high throughput, while 8.7 hours is reported to lose roughly one third of trips.
A river-length increase from 257 to 258 miles is reported to trigger another roughly one-third loss.
The preferred synthetic scenario reports 659.371 trips and approximately 98.8 percent campsite-night efficiency.
Increasing motor share changes reported trips by less than a four-percent decrease to a 2.3-percent increase across the tested range.
The clipped-Gaussian duration scenario loses roughly 27 to 30 trips relative to the uniform scenario.
Completed trips rise almost linearly with season length at about 3.5 trips per additional open day.
Within the stated non-threshold region, river length changes by up to 232 miles are claimed to change trip totals by only about eleven.
Trip totals rise with campsite count while the authors claim normalized efficiency remains nearly constant above the reachability floor.
The final recommendation prioritizes least remaining days, gives the less mobile craft the prose tie break, and tunes travel time to favorable thresholds.

contributions.summary: Represents boat trips and campsite occupancy as explicit Java state across day and site indices.
Uses remaining time and craft reach to drive a priority-based daily campsite scheduler.
Introduces recursive role swapping to repair local campsite conflicts without upstream motion.
Adds a pacing margin to the minimum average progress rule and links it to throughput and lateness.
Connects discontinuous simulation behavior to floor-function changes in reachable campsite count.
Normalizes trip totals with a campsite-night utilization reference.
Publishes the complete source code, enabling direct prose-code verification uncommon in the corpus.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The Summary gives judges the complete decision, algorithm, efficiency, sensitivity, and limitation map before details.
Before-and-after state diagrams make a difficult displacement algorithm inspectable when the implementation boundaries are also stated.
Complete source code permits unusually strong verification only if prose-code conflicts are actively checked rather than assumed away.

weaknesses.summary: The Summary states a magic-number comparison using D_O(Y) and D_O(Y-1), while the Memo and body use the motor reach at Y+1 versus Y; the conditions are not the same.
The Memo equates carrying capacity directly with Y campsites without defining whether capacity means nightly occupancy, concurrent boats, launches, completed trips, or people.
The prose calls the current site S_k while the displayed movement quantity is Delta S_k, and nearby text sometimes describes S_k as the daily advance.
The prose says schedule rows are campsites and columns are nights, but Java stores and accesses schedule[day][site].
The prose repeatedly gives oar boats tie priority, but Boat.compareTo() makes Motor sort before Oar in Java PriorityQueue.
The Memo's claim of the absolute minimum amount of interaction is unsupported by a proof, exhaustive search, or reported crossover optimum.
Crossover minimization is introduced as a core goal but is not included in the main optimization result and no crossover dataset is reported.
The Case 4 claim that an empty site must eventually be found is not a complete termination proof and the lastSite=-1 boundary is not handled.
reschedule() deletes a boat's historical cells without rolling back or recomputing later boats whose placements depended on those cells.
Season-end calls to reschedule() do not increment lateTrips or the lateness statistics, so final nonfinishers are omitted from that metric.
addBoats() uses continue for requests that cannot finish before season end, permanently removing them from the queue rather than recording rejection or censoring.
Running thousands of random request orders and keeping the best is a best-observed heuristic, not a proof of an optimal pre-schedule.
The paper supplies no random seed, frozen configuration, raw run outputs, confidence interval, or uncertainty propagation for its reported averages.
The appendix main method performs one run, so it does not reproduce the stated ten data points with one thousand iterations per point.
m_C is measured in campsite indices, but the prose compares it with eight to fifteen percent of maximum travel distance without a consistent unit conversion.
The selected m_C=4 is not reconciled with the eight-to-fifteen-percent rule across campsite counts and craft types.
Magic and black-magic settings are inferred from floor jumps and simulation behavior; they are not a general optimality theorem.
M=182Y/Lbar is not rounded to an integer and therefore is a continuous reference, not a strict maximum count of complete trips.
Efficiency uses n times average trip length rather than exact occupied schedule cells even though the complete schedule exists.
For clipped Gaussian requests the authors acknowledge that the efficiency calculation is not accurate, yet compare it with the uniform case as if metrics were directly aligned.
Figure 4 labels its horizontal quantity as a ratio of motor boats to oar boats, but the 0-to-1 scale functions like a motor fraction.
The authors call high motor-share points inaccurate and provide no error bars, so the small fitted improvement is not securely resolved.
The reported 98.8 percent is utilization under synthetic demand and assumed geometry, not an empirical validation of river carrying capacity.
The statement that the best possible efficiency is around 99 percent is not derived as a formal bound.
The claim that river lengths from 25 to 257 miles differ by only about eleven trips lacks the complete scenario table and uncertainty needed to reproduce it.
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) remains negative, so the uniform trip-length expression has a rare out-of-range failure path.
countCrossovers() is not tested or formally justified and its nested ordering logic may duplicate or omit crossover events.
Linear extraction damages smart punctuation, inequality signs, ceil and floor brackets, mean bars, and two-dimensional formula layout; rendered pages are required for fidelity.
The internal boat states and labels in Figures 1 and 2 do not enter text extraction and cannot be reconstructed from captions alone.
Reference 5 loses an underscore in extraction; the web references lack access dates and Reference 2 lacks a publication year.
The source contains grammar and spelling defects including where for were, procede, addBoats()which, and a double negative in the rollback proposal.
The phrase move back means retreat from a preferred downstream site, not physical upstream travel, and can be misread against the no-backwards assumption.
Trips, completed trips, rescheduled trips, schedule occupancy, and seasonal capacity are not kept as consistently distinct output types.
First-come individualized demand and best-of-random pre-scheduled demand are mixed when interpreting optimality and efficiency.
The greedy priority and displacement procedure is not shown to maximize completed trips globally or minimize crossovers globally.
No target-river occupancy, failure, environmental, ecological, safety, or demand data calibrate the operating recommendation.
MOVEMENT_CONSTANT is declared as 4 but getPreferredNextSite() hard-codes +4, so changing the named constant does not change behavior.
MOTOR_SPEED=80 and OAR_SPEED=40 are daily distance limits although getSpeed() and earlier prose use mph language; the unit naming is ambiguous.
The Gaussian harness clips values to seven and nineteen, creating endpoint probability masses rather than sampling a mathematically truncated Gaussian.
The test harness prints diagnostics without assertions or nonzero failure status and does not validate distribution or campsite input, so it is not an automated regression test.

independent_extensions.summary: Adopt one canonical schedule orientation and document day, night, campsite, launch, exit, and completion indices with executable invariants.
Fix and test the craft tie comparator so prose, priority queue behavior, and recursive displacement use one declared rule.
Prove termination or replace recursive displacement with a bounded augmenting-path search that handles missing prior sites and full-capacity states.
Use transactional rollback or full forward recomputation after removal so later placements cannot depend on deleted history.
Compute exact occupied campsite-nights, completed trips, rejected requests, censored trips, reschedules, and crossovers from one typed run record.
Use fixed seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, machine-readable scenario grids, and uncertainty-aware threshold selection.
Replace console diagnostics with assertions and property tests for capacity, direction, reach, timing, uniqueness, comparator, rollback, and crossover invariants.
Sample a true truncated distribution, validate inputs, avoid Integer.MIN_VALUE arithmetic, and record the random seed and generated request manifest.
Calibrate campsite geometry, closures, group size, demand, trip completion, contact, safety, environmental limits, and manager objectives to the target river.
Generate the manager memo from typed outputs so capacity, threshold equations, units, priority rules, uncertainty, and caveats cannot drift from the implementation.
